events.text:
🇸🇦🇴🇲Saudi Arabia eyes Oman as hedge against blocked oil export routes
 
Iran’s shutdown of Hormuz and Ansar Allah’s targeting of Saudi assets along the Red Sea have put the kingdom’s economy on the brink of crisis, with over 40% of GDP, ~80% of export earnings and up to 90% of budget revenues coming from a resource Riyadh is now[ having trouble getting onto the world market](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75197).
Enter the Duqm route: a $7B, 1k km proposed mega pipeline to link oil fields in eastern Saudi Arabia to the safe, blockade-free port of the same name along Oman’s Arabian Sea coastline.
The existence of the project, currently in the feasibility study phase, was formally revealed by TotalEnergies CEO Patrick Pouyanne this week, although Israel’s influential Institute for National Security Studies think tank discussed the idea in a report dated September 17 – touting the project’s potential to get up to 7M bpd in Saudi oil out of the Gulf.
🔍There’s no official word yet from Oman, but the idea of building a pipeline from Saudi Arabia through the sultanate was first proposed in the early 1970s, and formally floated by Oman’s economy minister in 2021.
It never materialized due to Riyadh’s prized East-West Pipeline, potential engineering problems of a route running through the vast, potentially treacherous Empty Quarter desert, and Oman’s long tradition of neutrality and [willingness to cooperate with both Iran and the Arab Gulf powers](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75510).
A mega pipeline with the Saudis would be a major financial boon for Muscat, but would first have to overcome massive geopolitical and economic hurdles, including upfront capital costs, the issue of Oman’s aggressive push to become the world’s leading exporter of clean hydrogen fuels, and its agreements with [Iran regarding Hormuz](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74908).
Not to mention regional pipelines’ critical vulnerabilities to potential drone and missile strikes.

events.text:
🇨🇳 ⛴ China’s growing power projection prowess pushes top think tank to rethink US Navy’s entire Pacific strategy
 
The US Navy has run into a problem – China’s growing and increasingly sophisticated surface fleet, from the new Fujian supercarrier to the Sichuan amphibious assault/drone ship, and force multipliers like the KJ-600 AEW&C aircraft.
Together, these capabilities allow China to break out of the so-called ‘Island chain strategy’ that the US has been using since the 1950s to hem China’s navy into its home shores.
➡️To “hunt” these assets, the US will need “a combination of subsurface, land-based, air, cyber-electromagnetic, and unmanned capabilities,” and a shakeup of its entire naval posture and shipbuilding plans, the Center for Strategic & International Studies (a top Beltway MIC-linked think tank) urges.
CSIS recommends a buildup of US and allied nuclear and diesel-electric sub capabilities, heavy torpedoes, unmanned undersea vehicles, “land-based maritime strike networks along key maritime terrain” from Japan to the Philippines, plus air and space-enabled long-range anti-ship missiles, drone swarms and port-strike weapons.
💲 To create these “sustained maritime denial” capabilities, Congress is urged to deliver the necessary funding, and support aggressive drone, amphibious landing and Indo-Pac maritime sustainment project expansion, and refocus ship construction on unmanned vessels (to 300 manned, 300 unmanned by the 2030s, instead of the 381-134 now planned).
It’s unclear where the money for all these projects would come from. The $1.5T FY 2027 defense budget includes tens of billions for new naval drone capabilities, but it’s nowhere near enough to achieve the 300/300 ship plan CSIS proposes.

Yemeni Armed Forces spokesman Yahya Saree issued a video statement following the missile and drone attack on Saudi Aramco facilities in Riyadh, warning that further Saudi strikes on Yemen would bring further escalation.
💬 “We will continue to impose the equation of, siege for a siege, and, an escalation escalation for escalation,” Saree said.
He added that Yemeni forces would continue targeting Saudi troop buildups until “the aggression ceases and the siege on our beloved country is lifted.”
Saree said the Riyadh operation used ballistic missiles and drones and described the strikes as “precise and direct.”
